questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presented with a painful, red, purulent port site and fevers. He had pancreatic cancer and an implanted port for chemotherapy. On exam, the port site was erythematous, with a central area of fluctuance, and some visible purulence. His temperature was 37.2°C, heart rate 98 beats/minute, and blood pressure 108/64 mmHg. Investigations: Neutrophil count 7.2 ×109/L Alkaline phosphatase 95 U/L Empiric antibiotic therapy was started while plans were made for his port to be removed.
questions.lead_in: What antibiotic is an essential component of empirical treatment?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin Central-line associated infections are most commonly caused by gram-positive organisms, most notably Staphylococcus and Streptococcus spp. MRSA is sufficiently prevalent to warrant empiric coverage with vancomycin or another effective agent, and parenteral therapy should be considered until bacteremia is excluded.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q15

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with ESRD on hemodialysis and difficult intravenous access needed new intravenous access to be placed for daily administration of parenteral medications.
questions.lead_in: What type of intravenous catheter carries the highest risk of bloodstream infection?
questions.explanation: Nontunneled femoral CVC Risk of bloodstream infection from IV access varies based on type of catheter and site of placement. Non-tunneled CVCs (central venous catheters) have higher rates of infections than tunneled catheters, PICCs (peripherally inserted central catheters), and peripheral IVs. Femoral placement confers a higher risk of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) than internal jugular and subclavian insertions. Type of catheter: Peripheral IV < PICC < Tunneled central venous catheter (CVC) < Nontunneled CVC Site of CVC: Subclavian < Internal jugular < Femoral CVC
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q15

questions.stem: Catheter-retention in the setting of central lineassociated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is sometimes attempted depending on disease severity, alternative IV access options, and pathogenicity of the organism identified.
questions.lead_in: According to recommendations, long-term catheter retention may be attempted if blood cultures are positive for what organisms?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis IDSA guidelines suggest that long-term CVCs should be removed in the circumstance of a CLABSI from all of the organisms listed, apart from S. epidermidis . Catheter removal, however, in this circumstance can shorten the needed antibiotic duration and can reduce the risk of relapsed BSI from any residual biofilm formation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q16

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fevers, malaise, and redness around the site of a longterm indwelling IV line in place for cancer chemotherapy. She had a history of metastatic cervical cancer. She had no known drug allergies. On physical exam, some purulence was expressed from the IV line site. Investigations: Total white cell count 12.5 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL Platelets 55 ×109/L Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Gram-stain of exit site pus showed GPC in clusters Blood cultures obtained through both the longterm indwelling IV line, as well from a peripheral vein, were positive for Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibilities pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial empiric treatment of this patient’s bacteremia?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) must be covered empirically, pending sensitivities. Dalbavancin is not established for treatment of infections other than acute bacterial skin/skin structure infections. Linezolid should be avoided for treatment of line-related bacteremias due to inferior efficacy in that setting. Clindamycin is not as reliably active against MRSA as vancomycin and is not established as a preferred treatment for MRSA bloodstream infection. There are no apparent contraindications or concerns with using vancomycin in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q4

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman was reviewed in the intensive care with fever and hemodynamic instability. She was recently repatriated to a rehabilitation hospital in the United States from India, where she had been hospitalized for 3 months because of a cerebrovascular accident. She had a peripherally inserted central catheter for blood work, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube for supplemental alimentation, and an indwelling urinary catheter. Five days earlier, she had developed fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. She was started on meropenem and fluconazole. Investigations: PICC and peripheral blood cultures: positive for Candida haemulonii after 72 hours; susceptibility as follows: Agent Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) or Mean Effective Concentration (MEC) Interpretation Fluconazole 128 μg/mL Resistant Amphotericin B 2 μg/mL Resistant Micafungin 0.5 μg/mL Susceptible
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely correct identification of the organism?
questions.explanation: Candida auris Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen that causes otomycosis and invasive candidiasis. It is an important nosocomial pathogen, especially in some parts of the world where it has already established endemicity. Healthcareassociated outbreaks have been reported in the United States. C. auris will be misidentified by commercial identification systems. The Vitek-2 will usually misidentify C. auris as Candida haemulonii and sometimes as Candida famata; the API-20C system will misidentify C. auris as Rhodotorula glutinis, Candida sake, or Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The correct identification can be made through DNA sequencing or with matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q25

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man was reviewed with a 4-day history of fevers and hypotension despite empiric use of broadspectrum antibiotics. The man had presented to hospital 3 weeks earlier with profuse diarrhea and severe malnutrition. He had Crohn’s disease with short gut syndrome secondary to multiple bowel resections. He was initiated at admission on total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter. His antimicrobials were changed to meropenem and micafungin. Investigations: Total white cell count 20 ×109/L Platelet count 50 ×109/L Blood cultures (central and peripheral) no growth after 3 days CXR: bilateral airspace disease
questions.lead_in: What is the best next test to secure a diagnosis?

options.text: Blood culture inoculated onto Sabouraud dextrose agar
Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil

questions.explanation: Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil This is a case of disseminated Malassezia infection. Risk factors in this case include CVC and lipid infusions (TPN). Malassezia spp. are intrinsically resistant to echinocandins, thus a response to micafungin is not expected. Malassezia spp. are lipophilic, and all species but M. pachydermatis require exogenous lipids for growth. M. furfur is the most common pathogen involved in disseminated disease. Recovery from standard blood cultures is low unless the media is enriched with fatty acids, i.e., with olive oil, palmitic acid, Tween, etc., or with Dixon’s agar, which contains glycerol mono-oleate. Serum 1,3- β-D-glucan is a nonspecific biomarker of fungal disease. It is not particularly helpful in making a diagnosis. Panfungal PCR is not useful on blood because of the low burden of organisms in the total circulation. Serum CrAg is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcosis (including subclinical disease). It also can cross react with Trichosporon spp. in disseminated disease, although a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Trichosporonosis has been reported in neonates but is less likely than Malassezia disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q26

questions.question: A patient 10 days post op after insertion of a prosthetic knee. She develops a fever post for 24 hours. She has a PICC line in place and the surgeon orders the line to be removed. Prior to removal, the line is functioning well with no erythema or discharge around the site. Follow-up cultures are negative in the urine and blood. Tip culture is positive for MSSA. You are consulted for management of a "line-related infection".

parts.text: What 2 things would you advise the surgeon

cohort_answer.text: No evidence of systemic infection, removal of line is sufficient, no systemic abx needed. Evaluate knee as source of infection.

questions.question: CLABSI question. February: 15 positive isolates, 150 patients, 1500 patient days, 1000 central line days. March: 10 positive isolates, 150 patients, 2000 patient days, 1000 central line days.

parts.text: What was the rate of CLABSI in February (in standard units, per 100,000 central line days)
What is the catheter utilization ratio?
You find out that ALL of the CLABSI isolates are MRSA. What is the attack rate?

cohort_answer.text: Rate Feb: 15/1000 x 100000 = 1500 per 100,000 central line days (or 15 per 1000 central line days). Catheter utilization ratio (CUR) = catheter days/patient days = 2000/3500 = 0.57. Attack rate = new cases/persons at risk = 25/300 = 0.083 (8.3%)

questions.question: Central line infections in dialysis unit

parts.text: What is the central line with the lowest rate of CL BSI recommended for use in dialysis patients
Name 6 core IPAC measures to reduce BSI in a dialysis unit

questions.model_answer:
a) Lowest CLABSI-risk vascular access for dialysis: arteriovenous fistula (AVF) - preferred over grafts and especially over central venous catheters.
b) Six core IPAC measures: (1) hand hygiene before and after each patient contact/catheter manipulation (2) aseptic no-touch technique with chlorhexidine-based antiseptic for catheter insertion and at each dialysis session (3) antimicrobial/antiseptic ointment (e.g., povidone-iodine or polysporin triple) at the catheter exit site (4) 'scrub-the-hub' disinfection of catheter hubs before every connection/disconnection (5) minimizing catheter use by promoting permanent AV access (fistula/graft) and prompt catheter removal when no longer needed (6) staff training/competency assessment with ongoing infection surveillance and feedback.

questions.question: Hemodialysis unit and BSI.

parts.text: For a hemodialysis patient, what site of vascular access is associated with the lowest infectious risk?
What are 6 practices for a hemodialysis centre to reduce the risk of vascular access infections?

questions.model_answer:
a) Lowest infectious-risk vascular access: arteriovenous fistula (AVF).
b) Six practices to reduce vascular access infection risk: (1) hand hygiene before/after patient and catheter contact (2) chlorhexidine-based skin antisepsis for cannulation/catheter care (3) topical antimicrobial ointment at catheter exit sites (4) hub disinfection ('scrub the hub') before every catheter access (5) preferential use of AV fistula/graft over catheters, with catheter removal as soon as feasible (6) ongoing staff education and infection surveillance with feedback of rates.

questions.question: Blood stream catheter infections in hemodialysis patients

parts.text: What is proven to be the least risky vascular access and therefore is the recommended approach?
What are 6 infection control measures that can be taken to reduce catheter line associated bloodstream infections in the hemodialysis unit?

questions.model_answer:
a) Least risky vascular access / recommended approach: arteriovenous fistula (AVF).
b) Six infection control measures to reduce CLABSI in hemodialysis: (1) hand hygiene at each patient/catheter contact (2) chlorhexidine antisepsis for insertion and dialysis session catheter care (3) antimicrobial ointment at the exit site (4) hub disinfection before every connection/disconnection ('scrub the hub') (5) minimizing catheter dependence - prioritize AV fistula/graft placement and remove catheters promptly when possible (6) staff education/competency and surveillance with feedback of infection rates to the unit.

questions.question: ICU patient who is very sick and there is GNB growing in BCx. You want rapid diagnostic and susceptibility testing

parts.text: For enterobacterales, what 3 antibiotics can be tested by disk diffusion directly on a blood culture sample according to CLSI guidelines?
What is 1 non-enterobacterales bacteria to the species level for which this method also has valid breakpoints?
List 5 essential practices from the most recent IDSA/SHEA guidelines to prevent CLABSI during line insertion

questions.model_answer: a) Enterobacterales direct disk diffusion from positive blood culture (CLSI-validated rapid AST): ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, meropenem (piperacillin-tazobactam also validated). b) Non-Enterobacterales organism with valid direct-from-blood-culture breakpoints: Pseudomonas aeruginosa. c) Five essential CLABSI-prevention practices at insertion (IDSA/SHEA): (1) hand hygiene before insertion (2) maximal sterile barrier precautions (cap, mask, sterile gown/gloves, full body drape) (3) chlorhexidine (>0.5% with alcohol) skin antisepsis (4) avoid femoral vein in adults - preferred subclavian site (5) use a standardized insertion checklist/bundle with real-time observer.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 rapid AST (RAST) from positive blood culture protocol; IDSA/SHEA Compendium CLABSI prevention 2022 update.

questions.question: The nephrology unit has an increased rate of blood stream infections.

parts.text: What type of line has the lowest risk of CLABSI? (I think they wanted location)
What are 6 recommendations to reduce the CLABSI rate?

cohort_answer.text: Subclavian = lowest rate of infection. Recommendations: aseptic technique for insertion; handwash before insertion; sterile barriers (mask, cap, gown, sterile gloves, sterile drapes); minimize times accessed; daily chlorhexidine bathing in ICU patients >2 months of age; scrub port with friction immediately before access with appropriate antiseptic (chlorhexidine, 70% alcohol); prepare insertion site with >0.5% chlorhexidine+alcohol, must dry before insertion; daily audit to assess if line needed.

questions.question: A woman who was previously treated at another hospital presents with fever and sepsis with a central line. Blood culture is positive at 6 hours with a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: What is your next management steps for the catheter and for antimicrobial treatment?
Name a test to differentiate albicans vs non albicans, and indicate what the expected result is for C. albicans.
The isolate is non-albicans. Do you change anything in your management, and if so, what?

The candida is identified as C. haemulonii with high MIC to azoles, echinocandins and amphotericin. However, you do not believe this result. What do you suspect? Are there any special precautions to take?

questions.model_answer: a) Catheter management: remove the central line promptly (source control - candidemia mandates catheter removal); start empiric antifungal therapy immediately, do not wait for speciation. Antimicrobial: empiric echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin or micafungin) pending speciation/susceptibilities. b) Test to differentiate C. albicans from non-albicans: germ tube test - C. albicans is germ tube positive (forms a germ tube when incubated in serum at 37°C), whereas most non-albicans species are germ tube negative. c) If non-albicans: reassess antifungal choice based on species and susceptibility (e.g. C. glabrata/C. krusei have reduced fluconazole susceptibility - continue echinocandin; C. parapsilosis has relatively higher echinocandin MICs - consider fluconazole if susceptible); continue source control and ophthalmologic exam, echocardiogram if indicated for all candidemia regardless of species. d) Suspect laboratory misidentification of Candida auris (frequently misidentified as C. haemulonii by conventional biochemical/VITEK systems); given pan-resistant profile, confirm identification with MALDI-TOF or molecular sequencing. Special precautions: implement contact precautions and single-room isolation, notify infection control/public health (C. auris is a reportable, outbreak-prone organism), enhanced environmental cleaning given its ability to persist on surfaces and colonize skin.
